problem: People can attach AI tasks to their goals in Quest and schedule them, but nothing runs them: Quest queues the work and has no worker. The same gap exists for anyone who wants AI to keep working on their goals between conversations.
who_has_it: Quest users and teams who delegate research, drafting, checking and follow-up to AI, and the operators who would otherwise run those tasks by hand.
why_it_matters: Delegated work that never happens stalls the goals it was meant to move, and people stop trusting the app to act on their behalf.
why_hard: A useful worker has to understand each task in the context of its goal, use the person's own material, decide when to answer and when to do real work, stop at the right point, and report back, all safely and at a bearable cost.
existing_attempts: Doing the task by hand in a general chat assistant; scheduled scripts; each organization writing its own private worker (four separate copies of the same lane driver were written before QAR held one).

problem: A general assistant answers from general knowledge. It does not know the person's quests, plans, documents, past conversations or preferences, so its help is plausible but not theirs, and sometimes states things about their account that are not true.
who_has_it: Anyone asking AI about their own goals and work: Quest users in chat, teams with shared quests, people directing AI on a codebase or a corpus.
why_it_matters: Generic help has to be checked and corrected, which costs the time it was meant to save, and confident but ungrounded statements erode trust.
why_hard: The relevant material is spread across many sources, far larger than any prompt, changes constantly, differs per person and team, and must never leak from one scope to another.
existing_attempts: Pasting context into a chat; custom assistants with uploaded files; retrieval products over a single document store; memory features in chat assistants.

problem: An AI that may act on someone's behalf tends to one of two failures: it asks permission for everything, so nothing moves without a person, or it takes steps that only a person should decide (spending, sending, deleting, anything irreversible).
who_has_it: People and teams who delegate to AI, and the person accountable for what the AI does.
why_it_matters: Over-asking wastes the delegation; acting alone on the wrong things causes harm that cannot be undone.
why_hard: Which steps belong to a person depends on the action, the person, the organization and the moment, and the model's own wording cannot be trusted as the gate.
existing_attempts: Approve-every-step agent interfaces; fully manual workflows; fixed allow and deny lists of actions.

problem: Grounding, routing, deep work, escalation, a task executor, cost control: each product or team that wants AI help writes these again, privately, and the copies drift apart.
who_has_it: Developers of Quest and of any other product that wants goal-grounded AI help, including teams outside the organization that built QAR.
why_it_matters: Effort is spent many times over, improvements made in one copy never reach the others, and chat and scheduled tasks answered by different engines behave differently.
why_hard: Each consumer has its own data, storage, people and rules, so shared code must stay ignorant of all of them while still being useful.
existing_attempts: General agent frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, the OpenAI and Claude agent SDKs), which give building blocks but not a grounded, goal-aware engine with escalation and a task executor; copying code between repositories.

problem: Models, prices, tools and techniques change every few months, so a router, a retrieval method or a model choice that was right becomes wrong, and nobody notices until quality drops or cost rises.
who_has_it: The maintainers and operators of QAR, and Joshua steering its quality.
why_it_matters: An engine that cannot follow the state of the art either degrades or needs rewrites, and quality decisions get made by habit.
why_hard: Comparing alternatives needs good cases, honest measurement and a way to switch, and language model output is noisy and costly to measure.
existing_attempts: Periodic rewrites; following public benchmarks; ad hoc evaluation scripts.

problem: Operators learn what AI work cost, and whether it was any good, only after the fact: a runaway run, a large model on an easy question, or a quiet drop in answer quality.
who_has_it: Operators paying for AI work, and people relying on its output.
why_it_matters: Spend surprises and silent quality loss both end the willingness to delegate.
why_hard: Quality is hard to measure automatically, cost depends on caching and vendor pricing, and both vary per task.
existing_attempts: Vendor billing dashboards, spend caps, spot checks by hand.

problem: A short chat message is sometimes handled the wrong way: a plain question starts expensive autonomous work, a request to change something only gets talked about, or a destructive request runs without anyone confirming it. A clear instruction can also get a clarifying question back instead of being done.
who_has_it: People chatting with the AI in an app, and teammates who queue requests for it.
why_it_matters: A wrong route either wastes spend and time, leaves the person's request undone, or acts irreversibly on something they only half meant. People stop trusting the assistant after one surprise.
why_hard: A message is short and ambiguous, the same words mean different things depending on the quest in view, and the cheap ways to decide (keywords) miss paraphrase while the careful ways (a large prompt per message) cost more than the answer is worth.
existing_attempts: Keyword rules, one large classification prompt, a planner loop that decides step by step, and a cheap pre-stage that settles clear requests before the planner. Chat products elsewhere ask the person to pick a mode.

problem: Replies state things that are not in the person's own account, or miss facts that are, because the AI answers from general knowledge, from the wrong slice of data, or invents a link or claim that no source supports.
who_has_it: People who ask the AI about their own goals, notes and decisions.
why_it_matters: A confident answer about someone's own work that is wrong or unsupported is worse than no answer: the person acts on it, or has to check every line themselves.
why_hard: The account is large and changes constantly, relevant evidence is spread across sources, a model fills gaps fluently, and a fabricated link looks exactly like a real one.
existing_attempts: Retrieval over files, databases and other sources before the model answers; a verifier that checks claims; stripping links that cannot be confirmed; retrieval-augmented generation in general.

problem: A request to change a quest leads to changes nobody asked for, to only part of what was asked, or to the same change made twice.
who_has_it: People and teammates who let the AI edit goals, notes and experiments for them.
why_it_matters: Quest data is the person's own plan. An unrequested write is hard to notice and undo, and a partial change leaves the plan inconsistent while the reply claims success.
why_hard: A change request is natural language mapped onto many tools with many arguments; a model tends to be helpful beyond the ask, multi-step requests need every step done once, and a retry after a timeout can repeat a write.
existing_attempts: Tool schemas with explicit arguments, a confirmation step for destructive actions, a scoped writer that only performs the one named operation, and database-level checks of the final state.

problem: People give the same correction again and again because the AI does not keep what they said, or keeps it but does not apply it where it bears.
who_has_it: Anyone who works with the AI repeatedly and tells it how they want things done.
why_it_matters: Repeating a correction is the clearest sign the assistant is not learning, and it costs the person's patience every time.
why_hard: A correction must be stored exactly as said, separated into a one-time request versus a standing rule, turned into guidance, and shown only on the turns where it applies; showing every rule on every turn would bury the prompt.
existing_attempts: Memory features in assistants that store notes; hand-written system prompts; custom instructions a person edits themselves.

problem: A follow-up such as "and the other one?", or a message sent while the AI is still working, is treated as a fresh start, so the person has to restate what they just said.
who_has_it: People in an ongoing conversation or watching a long run.
why_it_matters: Conversation is how people expect to work with an assistant. Restating context makes the assistant feel like a form, and a message that arrives mid-run and is ignored wastes the finished work.
why_hard: The follow-up shares no words with what it refers to, the right earlier turn must be found without mixing in other quests, and a running worker cannot always be re-prompted while it is in flight.
existing_attempts: Replaying the full history into every prompt, summarising old turns, a warm-start store of the cards last used, and an inbox that surfaces new messages at the next decision point.

problem: Prompts grow past what the model window or the budget allows, or repeat the same block, so calls fail, cost more than expected, or bury the relevant part under noise.
who_has_it: Operators who pay for model calls and developers who assemble prompts.
why_it_matters: One real incident produced a prompt larger than any model could take. Overflow fails a turn outright, and duplication wastes money on every call it touches.
why_hard: Prompts are assembled at many points from many sources, each growing independently; budgets depend on the model window and on price; and what to drop first when over budget is a policy choice.
existing_attempts: Hard character caps at some points, summarising, deduplication in some assemblers, and manual trimming after an incident.

problem: Context cards drift from the sources they describe: a file changes or disappears and the card still says the old thing, and when a card backend is unreachable the AI loses its cards or silently drops writes.
who_has_it: Operators and developers whose AI reads cards instead of the original sources, and the people relying on its answers.
why_it_matters: Stale context produces confident answers about things that are no longer true, and a silent lost write means a correction never lands.
why_hard: Checking every source on every turn is too slow, cheap checks (size and time) can be fooled, a pointer inside a card may name data the library cannot read itself, and outages are rare enough to be untested.
existing_attempts: Rebuilding all cards on a schedule, size-and-time checks, content hashes, serving the last known cards when a backend fails, and leaving pointers unresolved.

problem: The card or passage that would answer a question exists, but it is worded differently from the question, so keyword search does not surface it and the answer is built without it.
who_has_it: People asking questions in their own words, and developers tuning retrieval.
why_it_matters: A relevant fact that is never seen is the same as a fact that does not exist: the answer is incomplete without anyone knowing.
why_hard: Meaning-based search finds paraphrases but costs an embedding model and latency, keyword search is fast and exact but brittle, and the best mix differs by corpus.
existing_attempts: Keyword and inverse-document-frequency scoring, embedding search with a vector store, hybrid fusion of both, and letting the model widen the query.

problem: Answering from the live web risks fetching addresses that should never be fetched, paying again for the same search, or returning the wrong passage from the right page.
who_has_it: Operators who allow web access and people who ask questions the account cannot answer.
why_it_matters: A fetch into an internal address is a security hole, repeated search spend is a quiet cost, and a wrong passage looks authoritative.
why_hard: Pages are untrusted and large, search vendors differ in price and quality and may not be configured, and redirects and name resolution can move a safe address to an unsafe one after it was checked.
existing_attempts: Search vendor APIs, plain page fetchers, caching of fetched pages, and allow and deny lists of addresses.

problem: Long autonomous work can run without bound, get stuck, repeat the same action, wait forever on a person, hit a usage limit unnoticed, or be killed while a slow build or download was actually still making progress.
who_has_it: Teammates who hand the AI a multi-step job, and operators who pay for it to run.
why_it_matters: A stuck run burns spend and blocks the person; a wrongly stopped run throws away work that was nearly done. Both erode willingness to delegate.
why_hard: From outside, a quiet worker looks the same whether it is thinking, waiting or dead; a worker process cannot always be re-prompted; and every stop rule has false positives and false negatives.
existing_attempts: Wall-clock timeouts, turn caps, a reviewer that reads the live log, supervisors that intervene on drift, and killing by hand.

problem: A run reports that it finished when the written goal was not met, or describes work that was never executed.
who_has_it: People who read the report instead of the work, and the reviewers who approve on it.
why_it_matters: A false done is the most costly kind of error because nobody looks further, and the gap is found later by someone who then distrusts every report.
why_hard: Models write fluent summaries of intended work, the done-standard is prose that has to be checked against real state, and the check itself can be gamed by the same phrasing.
existing_attempts: Goal-verification passes, a separate verifier model, deterministic checks of final state, and human review of the output.

problem: A person waiting on background work cannot tell what is happening, or is flooded with every internal step and cannot find the one thing that needs them.
who_has_it: People and teammates watching a live chat or a background run.
why_it_matters: Without readable progress people either interrupt work that was going fine or miss the moment they were needed.
why_hard: The same event stream suits a live viewer, a background milestone feed and a log, and which events matter depends on the mode.
existing_attempts: Raw log tailing, spinners, per-step messages, and a final summary only.

problem: Steps that only a person should decide (spending, sending, deleting, anything irreversible) are sometimes taken without them, or are surfaced without the detail needed to decide, or are dropped without anyone noticing.
who_has_it: The person responsible for the account or quest, and teammates asked to approve.
why_it_matters: An irreversible act taken for a person erodes trust permanently, and an approval request they cannot act on is the same as none.
why_hard: The model must recognise a human-only step by judgment, not a word list; the request must carry enough context to decide; and the delivery path differs by host application.
existing_attempts: Always confirming everything, denylists of risky words, review queues outside the assistant, and asking in free text.

problem: Operators learn what AI work cost only after it has been spent, and a runaway loop, a long prompt or an overloaded host can burn a daily allowance or fail other jobs.
who_has_it: Operators who pay for model calls and teams who share one allowance.
why_it_matters: Spend is the clearest limit on how much the AI can be used at all. A surprise bill or an exhausted allowance halts everyone's work.
why_hard: Prices change, cost is only known after tokens are counted, work arrives from many lanes, and an overloaded machine needs a pause that does not flap.
existing_attempts: Provider dashboards read after the fact, a hand-kept price table, fixed daily caps, and manual restarts.

problem: Most turns are easy yet are served by the largest model, or the cheapest model is used for work it cannot do, so quality or cost is wrong for the task.
who_has_it: Operators who pay for the calls and people who feel the quality.
why_it_matters: Model tier is the biggest lever on both cost and quality, and a fixed choice is wrong for most turns one way or the other.
why_hard: Difficulty is only known after trying, model names and releases change often, a tier can run out mid-day, and an outage should wait instead of failing.
existing_attempts: One configured model for everything, hand-picked per feature, and a fallback chain on error.

problem: One model vendor's outage, quota or price change stops all AI work, and moving to another vendor means code changes.
who_has_it: Operators and developers who run the AI in production.
why_it_matters: AI work is part of daily routines, so a vendor stoppage becomes a team stoppage, and lock-in removes bargaining power on price.
why_hard: Vendors differ in model names, error shapes, limits and features, so a swap touches many call sites unless the call surface is one interface.
existing_attempts: Vendor SDKs used directly, wrapper libraries, and manual failover scripts.

problem: A public repository grown from private code can leak keys, real machine paths, real ids or real addresses, and nobody notices until it is published.
who_has_it: Maintainers and the organisations whose private details could leak.
why_it_matters: A leaked secret cannot be unpublished, and history keeps it.
why_hard: Secrets take many shapes, a placeholder looks like a secret, and the leak is introduced by an ordinary edit.
existing_attempts: Manual review before commit, vendor secret scanners on history, and resetting history once.

problem: A developer embedding the library cannot tell which names are stable, how to configure a lane, whether the examples still run, or where to look, so integration is trial and error.
who_has_it: Developers and operators adopting the library, and newcomers reading it.
why_it_matters: A library nobody can adopt confidently stays single-consumer, and every undocumented behaviour is a future outage in someone else's system.
why_hard: Documents and examples rot as code changes, configuration comes from files and environment with an order of precedence, and a typo in a setting should fail early instead of silently doing nothing.
existing_attempts: A README, a tutorial, a reference of environment variables, hand-checked examples, and reading the source.

problem: A task someone queued for the AI can be lost, run twice, run before its time, run by the wrong persona, or end with no report.
who_has_it: Teammates who queue work and the operators who run the worker.
why_it_matters: Queued work is how people delegate. If a task sometimes vanishes or runs twice, nobody can rely on delegating.
why_hard: Several workers poll the same queue, claims race, tasks have schedules and personas, and the worker can crash between claim and report.
existing_attempts: A single worker, a database claim flag, manual re-queueing, and a log read by a human.

problem: Recurring background passes can work when the person's settings say they should not: past the daily budget, on a day nobody is rostered, or without a cadence being due.
who_has_it: People who set an autopilot cadence and budget for their quest.
why_it_matters: An autopilot that ignores its settings spends money and writes to a quest nobody asked it to touch, which breaks the promise of the setting.
why_hard: The decision depends on budget, cadence, a pending run-now request, reactive triggers and a roster, and it must be made before any goal is read or any model is called.
existing_attempts: A cron schedule, a global on or off switch, and per-run checks inside the pass.

problem: People ask for the same operation again and again, and each time the AI searches and plans from scratch at full cost, while what it learned about their habits is lost on restart or mixes between people.
who_has_it: People with recurring routines and operators paying for repeated planning.
why_it_matters: Repeated work is the most avoidable spend, and an assistant that never recognises a habit feels like it has no memory.
why_hard: A near miss must not trigger a write, a recipe must produce the same result as the slow path, and what is learned must be stored per scope and survive restart.
existing_attempts: Saved prompts, macros the person writes, and caching of model replies.

problem: AI collaborators produce changes without naming the problem, the ideal or a metric, duplicate what already exists, or add structure whose cost outweighs its benefit.
who_has_it: The reviewer directing AI work, and teammates who rely on the result being maintainable.
why_it_matters: Unstructured AI output multiplies faster than people can review, so the structure that makes it improvable is lost.
why_hard: Following a principle is behaviour, not vocabulary: an assistant can use the right words without the right action, and the right action sometimes is to add nothing.
existing_attempts: Written guidelines in instruction files, review comments after the fact, and templates.

problem: A grader for AI replies rewards the right words without the right behaviour, or was calibrated only against its own author's labels, so passing scores mean less than they appear to.
who_has_it: Maintainers who rely on behaviour scores and the reviewer whose judgment the grader stands for.
why_it_matters: A grader that can be fooled makes every behaviour score meaningless, and improvements to the AI chase the grader instead of the intent.
why_hard: Natural language answers can satisfy a rubric on the surface, the same author writes the cases and the checks, and a human reference is expensive to collect.
existing_attempts: Regex and keyword checks, model graders with rubrics, and spot checks by hand.

problem: A live two-way chat over an external channel can drop, duplicate or reorder messages, or break when a payload arrives in an unexpected shape.
who_has_it: Operators who connect the AI to a chat gateway and the people typing in it.
why_it_matters: A conversation with a missing or doubled message is confusing, and nobody can tell which side lost it.
why_hard: Gateways differ in payload shape, delivery guarantees and reconnect behaviour, and a live gateway is rarely available for tests.
existing_attempts: Using the gateway's own SDK directly, and polling for new messages.

problem: Data from one user, team or quest reaches another one's prompt or store, through retrieval, caches, conversation recall, shared stores or the sources fed to the AI.
who_has_it: People whose private notes and decisions could be shown to someone else, and the operators responsible for them.
why_it_matters: A cross-scope leak breaks the one promise a personal assistant must keep, and one incident is enough to end trust.
why_hard: Every read path, store and cache has its own scope key, new paths are added all the time, and a leak is silent: the answer simply contains the wrong person's fact.
existing_attempts: Row-level filters in the database, per-request scope arguments, and review of each new path.

problem: A small model call used to settle one narrow question (reach, quest choice, overseer signal, sufficiency) can return a malformed, hallucinated or missing verdict, and a wrong verdict silently changes the turn.
who_has_it: Developers who rely on cheap judgments inside a pipeline, and the people whose turns they change.
why_it_matters: Narrow judges run on most turns, so even a small error rate shows up daily, and an unusable verdict that is trusted corrupts the whole turn.
why_hard: The model's output format drifts, the verdict depends on the evidence the question was given, and the fallback when it fails must be safe and cheap.
existing_attempts: Strict output schemas, retries, defaulting to the conservative answer, and larger models for the judgment.

problem: Replies, experiments and finished work are chosen and judged from the quest alone, never from the top intent and metrics the quest serves, so effort drifts from what the person cares about most and gaps under an intent go unnoticed.
who_has_it: Anyone with top intents above their quests, and maintainers iterating on a repository's solutions.
why_it_matters: The work done is not the work that matters, and nobody is told that an ideal has no solution, a solution has no quest or a metric has no data.
why_hard: The why lives in a specification that no prompt used to read, and adding it naively inflates every prompt and charges users who have no intents.
existing_attempts: Life intents specifications (written, never read by anything that does work); generic standing instructions in every deep run.

problem: Quest relies on a few core machine-learning tasks in many places: classifying a quest or an input (which quest, which kind of ask, which route) and recommending (which goal, step or quest comes next). Each has had alternative implementations, but QAR's records do not name them as one solution, so no alternative is compared on a metric.
who_has_it: Quest users and the team that chooses between implementations.
why_it_matters: These tasks sit under many features, so one weak or unmeasured choice degrades every place that uses it, and a better alternative cannot be adopted by evidence.
why_hard: The tasks look different at each call site (a router label, a quest match, a ranked list), so it is hard to see they are one task and to build a shared case set with held-out labels.
existing_attempts: route-a-message measures message routing on labelled cases; the backend's intent classifier is measured with and without its registry. Which-quest classification has two rankers (quest_selection.py and quest_candidates.py), area-of-life classification has a vector match plus older thresholded alternatives, and intent and period recommendations are single model prompts; none of these is measured on labelled cases.

problem: A new request or input arrives and the system cannot tell which of a project's intent specifications (problems, ideals, solutions, implementations, metrics) concern it, so it either loads none, loads all, or relies on whichever the person remembers to mention.
who_has_it: Any run that should act by a project's specifications (an autopilot pass, a chat turn, a task on a goal), and the person whose intent the specifications record.
why_it_matters: Work that ignores the specified intent drifts from it; work that loads every specification spends the context budget on records that do not apply and buries the ones that do.
why_hard: A request rarely uses a record's words, so lexical match alone misses and semantic match alone returns near neighbours that do not apply; the final choice needs judgement, which costs a model call per candidate unless batched; and the model can name a record that does not exist.
existing_attempts: Context-card retrieval over files (core-context-selection) with TF-IDF and a model filter; the vector context assembler; reading the whole specification tree; the ESOI library's own non-AI specification index (esoi spec index), which this solution consumes.

problem: An agent asked to answer or work from a person's own material has to find the relevant part of it first. With nothing kept between runs it re-discovers the same files and facts on every run (the planner asks what to read, retrieval searches, the loop re-plans), which costs tokens and latency, can miss what an earlier run already found, and leaves no record of where an answer came from.
who_has_it: People whose quests, notes, documents and code the AI works from, and the operators who pay for every run.
why_it_matters: Grounding is what makes help the person's own rather than plausible general help. Paying the full cost of discovery on every turn makes grounding slow and expensive, and an answer that names no source cannot be checked or corrected.
why_hard: An always-loaded preamble is guaranteed but identical for every task, so it cannot carry task-specific pointers without bloating; reactive exploration is task-specific but expensive and thrown away after each run; a summary handed from a finder agent to a reasoning agent loses information at the handoff (docs/context-assembly.md, The problem and the Data Processing Inequality section); and whatever is kept goes stale as its sources change.
existing_attempts: Always-loaded rules files, reactive gather-and-replan through the retrieval adapter, a separate context-finder agent, and full-corpus retrieval on every turn.

problem: A card store grows far past the distinct content of its corpus. In copy mode a store nested in another store's corpus copied that store's cards under a namespaced id on every bootstrap pass, copies of copies were kept, and each pass stacked another namespace, so two real stores reached 8,557 and 32,070 cards on 2026-10-05 for corpora that need hundreds, and a search over them took minutes. A terminal chat log of 2026-10-21 reported a vector seed of 142,781 items, a figure not yet explained: the same evening both live stores held about 4.4k cards (the chat log's line 'Card store has 4380 cards').
who_has_it: Operators of lanes whose corpus root contains, or sits inside, another lane's store, and every person waiting on a turn whose context assembly scans the inflated store.
why_it_matters: Every card is scored, fingerprinted, kept fresh and embedded, so cost and latency grow with the copies while the knowledge stays the same; duplicates crowd the right card out of the few in view; and a lane cannot tell which copy is current.
why_hard: Each copy looks like a legitimate single import when seen alone; the original may be unreadable or gone, so removing a copy can remove the only one; taught and externally managed cards must survive any cleanup; and a fixed card quota would cut real knowledge from a large corpus.
existing_attempts: Mounting stores in place instead of copying them (docs/context-card-stores.md), context migrate-imports and merge-into, the card quarantine tool (scripts/quarantine_cards.py), the bootstrap guards and the card limit with its notice (committed 2026-10-22), the tidy at open (on in the runner's builders), and the repository tidy for a store on any repository, which on the Quest backend or Qdrant plans by default and, when the lane opts in, deletes after a full local export (adapters/card_store_tidy.py).

problem: A run's context comes from two retrieval pipelines that repeat the same stages separately: context card selection (keyword IDF, vector search, weighted reciprocal-rank fusion, then a cheap-model filter and consolidation) and ESOI record selection (field-weighted TF-IDF, an optional vector search, reciprocal-rank fusion, then a gated cheap-model choice). They keep separate indexes, budgets and output shapes, and only the card result is put into a run's context: ESOI records reach a run only through tools it has to think to call, or as a lexical-only slice for a deep goal, so the problem, ideal and metric a run serves are often not in view.
who_has_it: Every run that should act by a project's specifications, the developers who tune two pipelines for one job, and the operators who pay for two searches.
why_it_matters: A run that does not see the problem, ideal and metric it serves cannot aim its work at them or report against them; two pipelines double the tuning, the defects and the model calls; and two budgets cannot trade a weak card for a strong record.
why_hard: Cards and records differ in shape (pinned files and typed references against fixed fields and links), in scope (quest fences against one repository root) and in where they live (card repositories against esoi/*.csv); a merged ranking must not lose quality on either existing metric; and copying records into a card store would duplicate them, the cause of store inflation.
existing_attempts: select-context for cards; spec-selection behind the find_specs, related_specs, intent_specs and show_spec tools; the iterate-by-spec slice before a deep goal (lexical only); the ground-in-intent frame for autopilot passes.

problem: Whether a run improved anything is recorded only in part and only for a while. A deep run records a metric reading before and after (the record_metric_result tool and GoalMetrics) into a per-run file of readings in a temporary folder that is cleared after two days, and the task report carries it to Quest; but nothing says what the run moved, the reading never reaches the record it concerns, a card's last_outcome comes from the kind of turn rather than from any metric, and when the work shows a record is wrong or missing nothing makes the run fix it. Improvement is hoped for rather than checked per run.
who_has_it: The person who owns a project's specification and wants every run to move a metric, the AI runs that cannot see what earlier runs on the same record achieved, and reviewers deciding what to change next.
why_it_matters: Progress over time needs each iteration to leave what it learned where the next one starts; a reading that expires, or a needed specification change mentioned only in prose, is lost, and the same work is done again.
why_hard: A run may have no offline arm to measure with; a change made only through a shell command is not counted; some words in the records are the owner's own (an intent's vision statement, the ideals the owner wrote) and should change only by the owner's choice; and a new file per run would scatter the record instead of keeping one source of truth.
existing_attempts: The record_metric_result tool and the per-run file of readings it writes (the metric ledger of docs/metric-results.md), metrics and metric_missing on the task report (runner/executor_reporting.py), the iterate-by-spec slice and write-back, the results log written by esoi run, the tracking_status, tracking_owner, tracking_updated and tracking_notes columns of each record's row in esoi/tracker/ (the review files esoi tracker build writes, one row per record, whose tracking columns are kept for people to fill), and a card's usage_count, last_outcome and provenance.

problem: A person or a run about to build or change something does not identify the solutions that already cover it or constrain it. The evolvable-structure skill names four structural risks of this kind, recorded here as its sub-problems R1 to R4: a solution that duplicates an existing one (esoi-r1-duplicate-solution), an existing solution's benefits not leveraged (esoi-r2-overlap-not-leveraged), solutions that must change with something else not noticed (esoi-r3-co-change-missed), and a solution used where it should not be (esoi-r4-solution-misused). The former area column grouped solutions under numbered names that closed none of these risks.
who_has_it: AI runs and people that write or change code and records in the project, and the people who rely on what the existing solutions guarantee.
why_it_matters: Duplicated solutions drift apart and double the upkeep; a change that skips a constraining solution breaks a guarantee (a budget, a scope fence, a consent step) without any check noticing until it fails in use.
why_hard: The constraining solutions are often in a different problem's tree from the change, so links from the change's own problem do not reach them; names and search find solutions by topic, not by the risk a change carries; and a grouping added for tidiness becomes decoration that closes no risk.
existing_attempts: The former area column; the top problems each solution's problems roll up to; sub-intents; spec-selection's search over the records; reading every solution.

problem: R1: Adding a new solution that duplicates an existing one.
who_has_it: Anyone, a person or an AI run, who writes a new solution in a project's records or builds a new mechanism in its code.
why_it_matters: Two solutions for one purpose drift apart, double the upkeep and split the metric's evidence, so neither improves as fast as one would.
why_hard: The existing solution is often named for a different problem or in different words, so the author does not find it by name or topic; it can sit in another intent or another project.
existing_attempts: Reading every solution; spec-selection's search over the records; the tags of tag-solutions, which list the solutions that carry the same risk.

problem: R2: Not leveraging the benefits of an existing solution, such as partial overlap of purpose.
who_has_it: Authors of a new solution or implementation whose purpose overlaps part of an existing one.
why_it_matters: The new work rebuilds guards, budgets or interfaces that already exist and are already measured, and loses the improvements made to them.
why_hard: A partial overlap is not visible from the new solution's own problem, and a solution's interface may serve the need under another name.
existing_attempts: Implementations name the solutions they use (uses_solution_ids); principle 8 of the evolvable-structure skill, leverage existing structure; tags shared between solutions.

problem: R3: Not being aware of solutions that need to change definition or implementation due to something else changing.
who_has_it: Anyone changing a shared shape (a data format, an id rule, an interface, a setting) that several solutions depend on.
why_it_matters: One solution changes and the others that read or write the same shape keep the old assumption, so a guarantee breaks without any check noticing until it fails in use.
why_hard: The dependent solutions are usually under different problems, and links run from a solution to its problems, not between solutions that share a shape.
existing_attempts: Links between solutions only through uses_solution_ids; a tag naming the shape the solutions share.

problem: R4: Using a solution when it should not be for the particular use case.
who_has_it: Authors and runs that pick an existing solution for a new use case.
why_it_matters: A solution used where its Avoid line says not to does the wrong thing quietly: a cross-scope read, an unconfirmed irreversible act, unattended work on a conversational ask.
why_hard: The Avoid line sits in the solution's scoped purpose and is read only by someone who already opened that solution.
existing_attempts: Each solution's scoped purpose names what it avoids; tags that mark the solutions whose misuse is costly.

problem: A corpus's walk and its card sources read folders that are not its knowledge, and the worst of them look harmless by file count. A machine's daily backup snapshots, one dated folder per day and each a copy of the whole tree, each carried the card store the tree had that day: one backups folder held 155 stores with 760,608 cards, and any corpus rooted above it would have walked, imported and mounted every one of them. Earlier, on one real corpus of 81,465 indexable files, most of the files were a single vendored tree present twice and generated data. Before the risk gate, the folder review that decides this ran only above a 2,000-file floor and failed open: with no model, the review switched off or a failed call, every folder was read.
who_has_it: Operators whose corpus root sits above backups, snapshots, release archives, vendored checkouts or other stores; and every person whose turn is grounded in a store that took in copies.
why_it_matters: Each copy becomes cards that are fingerprinted, kept fresh, embedded and scored, so cost, time and store size grow with copies of the same knowledge; yesterday's copy of a file competes with today's in the few cards a run sees; and a single bootstrap over such a tree can take hours.
why_hard: A file count cannot tell a snapshot series from real material, and a snapshot looks like a legitimate nested store when seen alone. Asking a model about every file is the cost the decision exists to avoid, the model may be unavailable, and a rule that blocks too readily throws away real knowledge (a lane's one nested project is normal). Every card source (the file walk, nested store imports, ancestor imports, mounts) has to get the same answer, or the leak moves to the source that asked nobody.
existing_attempts: The skip list and extension filter; the model-judged folder review with its cached, human-editable verdicts (adapters/context_folder_review.py); the deterministic nested-repository and duplicate-tree safeguards; and the risk gate (adapters/context_risk_gate.py, commit ac61f64), one function every card source asks.

problem: Within one request, each planning step is a separate model call rebuilt from parts, not a continuation of the step before. From the second step on, the transcript and the whole context block (the resolved request, declined proposals, standing corrections, recent context and cards) are replaced by a note saying they were provided at step one, which a separate call never saw, and older observations are collapsed to one line, so a later step decides from the raw message and the newest reads alone.
who_has_it: People whose request takes more than one step: a question that needs several reads, a change that needs a lookup first, a long working session.
why_it_matters: A step that cannot see a refusal, a correction or what the request was resolved to mean can re-propose what was declined, contradict an earlier step or change subject. The same symptoms were seen in production across turns (one declined proposal re-issued ten times in one conversation, account state reported two ways within minutes), and the cross-turn cause was fixed for the first step of a request only.
why_hard: Re-sending the full context on every step was most of a turn's planner cost, which is why the note replaced it; a continued stream needs a provider call that carries many messages and caches their prefix, an admission rule so the stream does not fill with noise, and a way to correct an item already in it.
existing_attempts: A shared cached prefix of head and context layers for the calls of a turn (core/prompt_layers.py); the re-plan reference note (core/orchestrator_events.py, on by default since a token-usage pass); declined proposals prepended to the context block, which reaches the first step only; deep work, which already runs as one continued coding-agent session.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Proposed in the QAR anatomy review (Mind, Subconscious, Science, World, Body, Higher mind, Overseer).

problem: What of the person's own material enters a step's view is decided by position and size, not by what the request needs: cards are chosen once from the request text at the start, the newest few observations are shown in full and older ones collapsed, and a lookup's result is admitted whether or not it is what was asked for. A finding the goal turns on can be collapsed out while an irrelevant read stays in full, and a near miss can be treated as the thing requested.
who_has_it: People whose request needs several reads, and anyone whose account holds similarly named items.
why_it_matters: In production a request about one collection matched unrelated items by a loose pattern, analysed them, and recorded an outcome on the person's quest from the empty result. With a continued stream, anything admitted stays for every later step, so a wrong admission costs more than it does today.
why_hard: Relevance to the goal is a judgment, so admitting by it costs a model call or a learned scorer per candidate; thresholds are cheap but let near misses through; and the scope fence must hold on every path that admits anything.
existing_attempts: The card selector and its cheap-model filter at the start of a run; the recency window and one-line compression for observations (core/planner_context.py); the sufficiency and support checks on the answer; the scope tag predicate (core/scope_tags.py) applied per store.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Proposed in the QAR anatomy review (Mind, Subconscious, Science, World, Body, Higher mind, Overseer).

problem: A question about the world rather than the person's own material (health, training, research, experiences others have reported) is answered from the model's general knowledge or one web passage, with no sign of how strong the evidence is, and research sources a host already has are not consulted.
who_has_it: People who ask for advice or facts that turn on evidence, and hosts that hold research or experience data the AI could use.
why_it_matters: Advice given without its evidence cannot be weighed by the person, and two parts of the same product can give opposite advice: in production the chat advised skipping a long run while the background worker said to run it, and the person called it inconsistent.
why_hard: Evidence strength is rarely stated by sources, research sources differ per host and need their own access, the open web is cheap and fast while research sources are slower, and a model states general knowledge with the same confidence as a cited finding.
existing_attempts: Snippet-first web research with page extraction; the answer check that flags claims the turn's reads do not support and rewrites them once with their basis; the planner's habit of searching the web on most advice questions.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Proposed in the QAR anatomy review (Mind, Subconscious, Science, World, Body, Higher mind, Overseer).

problem: The AI states what it can and cannot do outside the host's own data without a source of truth for it: it describes a capability that does not exist, reports a setting as blocking when the setting was never read, or says outside work has started when nothing ran. It also says it cannot do something it can.
who_has_it: People who rely on the AI to say what it can do for them, and operators who connect external environments to it.
why_it_matters: In production one person was told about a submission script that does not exist, two others were told AI work was switched off in their settings when the request could have been done, and a reply announced a background task that was never queued. A false capability or a false blocker ends trust faster than a plain no.
why_hard: What is reachable changes per person, team and deployment (connected environments, allowlisted tools and servers, what a setting allows), the inventory lives in the host, and a model fills a gap in its prompt with a plausible capability.
existing_attempts: The host's reach summary and a stronger-tier reach judge before planning (core/reach_judge.py, off by default); the tool catalog's when-to-use text; the answer check that flags claims of unexecuted work.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Proposed in the QAR anatomy review (Mind, Subconscious, Science, World, Body, Higher mind, Overseer).

problem: What the AI says about the person's own account (which quests exist, what changed, whether a change ran) is re-derived each turn from whatever slice it read, and a change it made is not read back, so within one session it reports the same state two ways, repeats a change it already made, or proposes again what it said was done.
who_has_it: People who ask the AI to change their quests and then ask what state they are in.
why_it_matters: In production one account's quests were described as a single completed goal and then as four initialised quests within ten minutes, and the person asked what state the account was in four separate times. An assistant that cannot report its own state cannot be trusted to change it.
why_hard: The host's data changes from many places (the app, other people, background work), a card or cache of it lags, a read on every turn costs time, and a library that serves any host cannot assume one data model.
existing_attempts: A managed card per quest rebuilt on sync, through which a turn is grounded in its quest; live reads through the host's retrieval adapter; the quest change executor and its final-state metric; the answer check that flags claims of unexecuted work.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Proposed in the QAR anatomy review (Mind, Subconscious, Science, World, Body, Higher mind, Overseer).

problem: What is known across requests (what a quest has decided, declined and learned, what the person corrected, where the work is heading) is kept in several stores with their own keys, budgets and retrieval: past conversations, recent context, the feedback ledger and its guidance, the prediction store, the host's reflections and the quest cards. None of them holds the quest's standing view, so each request rebuilds it from fragments, background work can lack what the chat already knew, and each store needs its own scope fence.
who_has_it: People who work on a quest over many sessions, and developers who add a new place to remember something.
why_it_matters: In production a declined proposal kept returning until a separate fix routed declines to the planner, a background worker contradicted the chat because it lacked the chat's history, a new session inherited the previous day's subject, and one evening found the same cross-quest leak through three different stores in turn.
why_hard: Each store serves a different moment (a follow-up, a correction, a predicted next ask) under a different cost limit; merging them risks one large block in every prompt, a wrong summary that persists, or a single fence every path must remember to use.
existing_attempts: Cross-conversation recall, the scoped recent-context warm start, the feedback ledger and guidance provider, the prediction store, reflections read by the chat and the autopilot, quest cards, and the one shared scope tag predicate.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Proposed in the QAR anatomy review (Mind, Subconscious, Science, World, Body, Higher mind, Overseer).

problem: A run ends by handing the person steps the AI could have done itself, or is marked done with part of the original ask left undone, instead of continuing until the original ask is met.
who_has_it: People who delegate work to the AI and expect it finished, and the coordinators who follow up on it.
why_it_matters: The standard set in a founder's team meeting on 2026-10-27 is that the AI keeps going until the original ask is complete and a person is asked only for what only a person can do; every handed-back step is work a person must notice, understand and do.
why_hard: Telling a step only a person may take from one the AI could take is a judgment; the deep goal loop re-runs only while its verifier says the done-standard is unmet and stops at a cap or budget; a verifier that accepts a handback as done ends the run.
existing_attempts: The deep goal loop that verifies the done-standard and re-runs (queued tasks use it); the overseer's split between escalating to deep work and escalating to a person; the standing rule that only genuine forks go to a person.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Named in a founder's team meeting, 2026-10-27; proposed in the QAR anatomy review.

problem: The AI asks the person about implementation details they neither care about nor understand, and when told it should not have asked, does not learn which kinds of question to stop asking.
who_has_it: People who own quests and receive the AI's questions, most of all the busiest owners.
why_it_matters: Each needless question costs the person attention and hides the few questions that are really theirs; the AI is meant to learn from that feedback so everyone sees fewer of them.
why_hard: Whether a question is the person's to answer differs by person and by subject, the feedback is given in passing in free text, and a rule learned too broadly would stop real decisions reaching the person.
existing_attempts: The human escalation channel with its default and deadline; the feedback ledger and guidance that keep corrections; the rule that only identity, taste, irreversible acts and direction go to a person.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Named in a founder's team meeting, 2026-10-27; proposed in the QAR anatomy review.

problem: The same request is handled less capably through the chat than as a task sent to a coding agent: the chat's own loop is a partial agent harness, so it fails, stops early or asks again where the coding agent completes the work, while sending every request to the coding agent pays its slow, token-heavy context search each time.
who_has_it: Team members and users who work through the chat, and the operators who pay for coding-agent runs.
why_it_matters: People move to the surface that works and stop using the chat; in a founder's team meeting on 2026-10-27 a request to show a file on a server as a clickable link failed repeatedly in chat, while the task surface, which runs the coding agent directly, did such work.
why_hard: A full harness is large to build; routing every hard request to the coding agent needs routing close to perfect; answering from stored context needs that context to be found and current; an open-source harness would have to keep the library's scope fences and grounding.
existing_attempts: The message router and reach judge that send real work to a deep run; the context card store that lets simple requests skip the coding agent; small file reads and edits done without it; an earlier study of a coding agent's design for ideas.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Named in a founder's team meeting, 2026-10-27; proposed in the QAR anatomy review.

problem: Questions about how to use the app itself (how to do something, what a feature is for) should be answered from the product's own documentation, but that path is untested, the AI sometimes says it cannot do what it can, and many team members do not know what the AI can do for them.
who_has_it: New users finding their way around the app, and team members who use only a fraction of its features.
why_it_matters: Guiding a person through the app is one of the AI's largest opportunities: a person who cannot find a feature does not use it, and a person told the AI cannot do something stops asking.
why_hard: A usage question must be told apart from a request to act, with near-perfect accuracy to be trusted; the documentation must stay current with every release; and a person who is confused often does not ask the AI at all.
existing_attempts: The product documentation kept current by AI and included in the chat's context; the message router; tool descriptions with when-to-use text.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Named in a founder's team meeting, 2026-10-27; proposed in the QAR anatomy review.

problem: Most people have no external environment connected, so their delegated tasks can use only the app's own operations, its documentation, a review of their own data and web search, and that path has not been tested end to end.
who_has_it: Every user without a connected external environment, which is most of them.
why_it_matters: A delegated task is the product's promise of work done between sessions; if it only works where an external environment exists, most users never see it work.
why_hard: Tasks were built and proven on deployments that have an external environment; without one, every piece of work must be possible through in-app operations and web reads, and the AI must not offer or assume an environment that is not there.
existing_attempts: The queued-task runner; in-app operation tools; web research; the host's reach summary, off by default.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Named in a founder's team meeting, 2026-10-27; proposed in the QAR anatomy review.

problem: Advice and plans are given as one answer, not as the option most likely to work for this person with a metric to check it, and when the better option is unknown the AI does not propose or find an experiment that would settle it, though the app has an Experiments feature built for that.
who_has_it: People pursuing big goals who need to know what is most likely to work for them, not only what is plausible.
why_it_matters: What sets the product apart from a general chatbot is finding what is most likely to work for the individual and measuring it; an experiment the person carries out gives them a clear, grounded path and the metrics to track it.
why_hard: Most likely needs evidence, the person's own history and a metric, which are rarely all present; an experiment takes the person's time and consent; and a model answers fluently whether or not it has any of them.
existing_attempts: Experiment tools that find, create and change a quest's experiments when the person asks; experiment generation at the end of quest creation in the host; the intent frame and specification slice for background work.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Named in a founder's team meeting, 2026-10-27; proposed in the QAR anatomy review.

problem: The before-and-after reading of the relevant ESOI metric is enforced by code only on deep runs. Chat turns and other in-process work find no slice and take no reading; a request whose records hold no slice or no metric ends with nothing measured and nothing proposed; a reading that got worse is recorded and shown, but nothing acts on it; and a run that ends with no metric on record is marked and then forgotten.
who_has_it: The specification owner, who expects every request to apply the specification's metrics, and the people whose chat turns and small tasks are most of what the system does.
why_it_matters: A rule that holds only where the work is largest leaves most requests unmeasured, and a regression that is only displayed is a regression accepted; improvement over time needs every request held to its metric and every failure answered.
why_hard: A reading before and after costs time, and a chat reply cannot wait for an offline arm; many requests have no slice because the records are ambiguous or absent; proposing a metric must not invent a reading; and acting on a regression must not loop or undo what the person asked for.
existing_attempts: The slice of the specification, the meters, the result ledger and the one-nudge gate around every deep goal (core/spec_slice.py, core/metric_meter.py, core/metric_results.py, core/goal_metrics.py), shown in the terminal and the host's chat; the intent frame for quest-scoped prompts; the standing instructions that ask for a before and after.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Reworked 2026-10-28 by the specification owner's correction: the enforcer of ESOI metrics on every request. Open recommendation: keep as the enforcing role over iterate-by-spec rather than merge.

problem: Risky moments in a run (re-proposing a declined act, claiming work that did not run, handing back a step the AI could do, a wrong route, an irreversible act, a cross-scope read) are watched by one overseer that reviews a digest with one prompt on one tier, whatever the risk, and nothing shows which response works for which kind of risk.
who_has_it: People whose runs go wrong in a costly way, and operators who pay for review that may not help.
why_it_matters: The response that works differs by risk: on cheap-model routing, a reviewer handed every decision scored worse than no review, while the same model asked one narrow question of fact did well. A uniform reviewer spends on cases that need nothing and may argue with correct decisions.
why_hard: Each risk category needs its own cheap detector, its own labelled cases and its own comparison of responses; risky cases are rare, so a difference needs enough cases to be significant; and a response must never block a run when it fails.
existing_attempts: The digest overseer with a free non-model pre-filter before each consult; the reach judge; the answer check for unsupported or unexecuted claims; the scope tag fence; the declined-proposals block.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Owner's definition 2026-10-28: the overseer is risk management for the overall metric, per risk category, by metric with statistical significance.

problem: A representative's high-level view legitimately spans its assigned quests and the intents above them, but the library's fence compares flat tag sets: an item is visible to a turn only when their tags intersect, or everywhere when it has none. Nothing can say visible to this representative's assigned quests and their ancestor intents, never to another representative's quests, a sibling intent or another person; and a representative's learned notes and context preferences carry no scope at all, so what it learned on one quest reaches every other.
who_has_it: People and teams whose AI representatives are assigned several quests under nested intents (a life intent, an organisation, a product, its quests), all of whom rely on what is learned in one place staying there.
why_it_matters: The same cross-quest leak was found through three stores in one evening, and an evaluation account's representative notes rewrote answers about other quests; a view at an intent level widens what may be read, so without a hierarchy-aware fence it widens what can leak.
why_hard: The hierarchy lives in the host and differs per person and product; a parent link is active only while both sides state it and can be withdrawn; intents belong to a person, a team or an organisation with their own visibility; untagged legacy items stay visible by design; and every store that keeps context across turns must apply the same rule.
existing_attempts: The flat scope tag predicate applied in each store (core/scope_tags.py); the host's rule that a linked neighbour intent is shown only as far as its owner revealed; per-store fences added after each leak.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Owner's correction 2026-10-28: the higher mind belongs to an AI representative and its assigned quests, placed in the intent hierarchy, not to one quest.

problem: Which AI representative handles a message, a queued task or an autopilot pass is decided in three places by three rules (the host's chat classifier among a quest's assigned representatives, the task runner's precedence of assignment field, explicit ask and domain cards, and the autopilot roster by day), with no shared definition of the right representative, no labelled measure of how often it is right, and no rule that work spawned from a thread keeps that thread's representative. A quest can have several representatives, each with its own higher mind, so a wrong choice also grounds the request in the wrong view.
who_has_it: People and teams whose quests have more than one AI representative, and anyone who delegates work from a chat.
why_it_matters: In production a chat's turns ran as the person's default representative while the tasks they spawned ran as two other personas, with a different voice and different evidence in one thread, and the person called the advice inconsistent. Choosing the representative decides whose role, notes and long view ground the work.
why_hard: The fit between a request and a representative depends on roles written in free text, the quests each is assigned and what the person asked for; a bare mention of a name must not count as asking for it; a representative may be visible to one member of a team and not another; and asking the person every time is its own failure.
existing_attempts: The host's fast-model classifier that picks among a quest's assigned representatives and falls back to the person's default; the task runner's persona resolver (runner/personas.py); the autopilot roster with per-representative days and instructions; per-viewer visibility of representatives.
tracking_status: unconfirmed: for the specification owner to confirm
tracking_notes: Owner's direction 2026-10-28: a quest can have several AI representatives, and representative selection is a key aspect of the library.

problem: The AI answers the request in front of it and lets the person's long-term goal go quiet, so each small task is done without the end in sight; the opposite fix, a plug for the goal in every reply, nags, hijacks a simple question or lands on a person who is in a hurry or upset.
who_has_it: Anyone using Quest AI on a quest that serves a larger intent.
why_it_matters: Unconfirmed, from the call: the assistant is meant to keep moving people forward, with the end in sight, at the intent level they are working at; an assistant that does not looks like any other chat AI.
why_hard: A pointer is right at one moment and wrong at the next (urgent, narrow, unrelated, emotional, already raised), the right level depends on what the person is doing, and every pointer must name the real next milestone and the real current reading, never an invented one.
existing_attempts: The reply voice already says to answer first and be proactive only where it is worth the person's time; nothing measures whether it points at the next milestone, or whether it holds back when it should.
